title: Before you go.
summary: New England family life, classic style, useful products, weekends away and an age-respectful high-support autism lens.
search: The original practical notesBefore you go.The questions to ask. The words to borrow.Open just the note you need. Copy it, edit it for your situation and keep personal information limited to what is useful. The practical detailsQuestions to ask and notes to borrow. Open whatever you need. Plan a day out Seven questions before you go A little more information before leaving the house can save a lot of guessing when you get there. When is it quieter?Ask about crowds, music, hand dryers, and scheduled events. Where can we take a break?Check for a calm space and whether you can leave and re-enter. What are the bathrooms like?Ask about privacy, space, and the specific facilities you need. What can we bring?Confirm food, drinks, communication devices, and familiar comfort items. How does the visit actually work?Check queues, parking distance, steps, seating, and any required waiting. Is the main attraction open?Confirm today's availability, hours, age rules, and access restrictions. What happens if plans change?Ask about cancellation, refunds, and a shorter visit before booking. ShareCopyPrint Ask for access A clear request can be short. Explain what gets in the way, say what would help, and ask for a reply in writing. A note you can borrow Hi, we're planning to visit [place] on [date]. A family member has a disability, and [barrier] makes it difficult to take part. Would it be possible to [specific adjustment]? Please let us know what you can arrange and who to ask for when we arrive. If that won't work, is there another option? A written reply would help us plan. Thank you! Copy this request Be specificCould we wait somewhere quieter until it's our turn?Could you send a few photos or tell us what happens during the visit?Can our support person stay with us?Could we have the instructions in writing too? You can begin with the access need. Your family's entire history needn't go into the first email. US guidance: businesses open to the public and effective communication. Duties and exceptions depend on the setting. This is a starting point for a request, not individual legal advice. Hotels and pools A lovely lobby is a bonus. A working pool and the right beds are rather more important. The room: what are the actual beds? Does the separate sleeping area have a door? “Suite” leaves a surprising amount unanswered.The pool: is it open on your dates? And the hot tub? Ask about hours, age rules, and water temperature if it matters to you.The timing: can you swim before check-in or after checkout?The food: what exactly is in the kitchenette? A fridge and microwave won't do the same job as a stove.The noise: ask about events, room location, and somewhere to take a quiet break.The bill: get the total with taxes, parking, fees, and deposits. Read the cancellation terms before paying. Hi, we're looking at a stay on [dates]. Could you confirm the beds and room layout, what's in the kitchenette, and whether both the indoor pool and hot tub will be open? We'd also like their hours and age rules, and whether we can use them before check-in or after checkout. Please include the total with mandatory fees, any deposit, and the cancellation terms. We also need [access adjustment]. Thanks so much! Copy the hotel questions Ask the property about your actual dates. An old pool photograph can only tell you so much. Support communication Please speak to the person. Give them time to answer. Those two things are a very good place to start. AAC means augmentative and alternative communication. Speech, vocalizations, gestures, signs, photographs, objects, writing, spelling, eye gaze, switches, low-tech boards and speech-generating devices can all be part of one multimodal system. Keep the person's communication method within reach. Ask before moving or touching a device.Leave time for a response before asking the question again.Offer choices the person can use, including “no,” “stop,” and “break.”Use language that respects their age. Speech alone doesn't tell you what someone understands. A note for a hostPlease speak directly to our family member and give them time to respond. They communicate using [method]. Please keep it available and ask before touching their device. It helps to [individual preference]. They may also need time to pause. Thank you for making room for this. Copy the communication note Read the full multimodal communication guide → Further reading: CommunicationFIRST, its guidance written by AAC users, and ASAN on autism. Understand ableism Ableism can show up in an ordinary exchange: talking over someone, dismissing an access request, or assuming a person won't enjoy an activity because they need help with it. Some autistic people need substantial support throughout their lives. They still have preferences, privacy, and every reason to be included. What that means hereInclude the person in the conversation.Speak to them, with the communication support they use.Allow a different sort of visit.A break, a shorter stay, or watching before joining in can make the day work.Keep support available.Comfort and communication shouldn't have to be earned.Let private moments stay private.A hard day doesn't need to become a public story. We write as a family. Autistic people speak for themselves, including through AAC, and their own words matter. ASAN on autism · CommunicationFIRST's wording guide If an access request is refused Ask for the reason in writing. It gives you something specific to respond to. Restate the barrier and the adjustment you asked for.Ask which policy applies, and whether another arrangement would work.Find out who can review the decision.Keep the dates and messages. Write down what happened while it's fresh. Thank you for getting back to us. The difficulty is [barrier], and we asked for [adjustment]. Could you explain why that isn't possible, share the relevant policy, and let us know whether an alternative would work? Who could review the request? We'd appreciate a written reply. Copy the follow-up For US rights guidance: businesses, government programs, and Massachusetts communication access. The rules depend on the setting; a refusal alone doesn't establish a legal violation. Make the day simpler One good thing is plentyPick the part of the day everyone is looking forward to. Leave space around it, and know what the shorter version looks like. Before the shoes go onConfirm the hours, parking, bathrooms, and food.Show what comes first, next, and afterward in a familiar way. Actual photos can help.Know where you can take a break, and how to get back to the car. For the bagA communication device and charger, familiar food and drink, a comfort item, spare clothes if needed, and the supplies in the person's usual support plan.There is no prize for staying longer than everyone wants to. Choices, routines & things to do Today's choices, pleaseA choice board needs to match what's actually available. For an ice-cream stop, that means today's flavors at the right shop.Offer a few clear choices, with words and useful pictures.Keep flavor, cone or cup, and size as separate decisions.A strawberry picture says more than a pink square.Include “something else,” “no,” and “finished.” Allow time to choose. A short plan for a new placeShow the place, who will be there, what happens, where a break can happen, and going home. Use real photos when you can. Leave room for things to change. Activities for teensStart with what interests them: swimming, animals, films, a walk, or making something to eat. The amount of help someone needs doesn't make their interests younger.Ask about group size, noise, pace, and whether a support person can join.Check the changing facilities and where to take a break.See whether a short introduction or trial visit is possible.Find a part of the activity they can choose and take part in, with the help they need. A note to hand overThe plan today is [activity and time]. Communication: [method and response time]. What helps: [specific support]. A break: [place or cue]. If plans change: [how to explain or contact us]. Please follow the existing support and emergency plans.Copy the handover note Share private care details securely with the people who need them. More on communication support. Clothes that feel right A beautiful sweater that nobody wants to wear is still a sweater sitting in a drawer.Start with the clothes that feel right. Then look at the details: the collar, the seams, the waistband, and whether the fastenings are manageable.Use measurements. One brand's medium isn't every brand's medium.Check washing and drying before buying.Build around a comfortable shape or color that already gets worn.Read the return policy, especially when ordering an unfamiliar fabric.Classic can be quite simple. Comfortable clothes, a useful layer, and no argument with the waistband.Build a useful wardrobe One family. Not the whole spectrum.We write about what we wear, where we go, what earns space in the house, and the practical side of life with profound autism. The point is not perfection. It is knowing enough to make a better choice before spending the money or loading the car.Our family experience includes profound autism and very high support needs. That gives us one specific lens - not ownership of autism, neurodiversity, or anybody else's story.What that means hereWe use profound autism descriptively for our family's support-needs reality. We know the term is contested. Some families and researchers find it useful; some autistic self-advocates strongly oppose it. We do not use it as a hierarchy of human worth.When we write generally, we usually use identity-first language such as autistic person, while respecting individual preferences when they are known. We welcome autistic and neurodivergent readers across support levels.Some details stay within our family. Useful does not require invasive.Read our language & representation standard Notes from New England A swim and a good lunchGive us somewhere to swim and something good to eat, and there is the beginning of a day out.It is tempting to add three more stops because they're nearby. They will still be there another day. Leave time to enjoy the thing you came for.Before leaving, check the opening hours, food, bathrooms, and somewhere to take a break. Keep a shorter version of the day in mind too.The questions to ask first The unglamorous questionsCan it go in the washing machine? Does the lid come apart for cleaning? Will it need a subscription after we've bought it?Those questions aren't much use in a beautiful photograph. They're rather useful once the parcel arrives.The same goes for meal kits. “Quick” can mean very different things once you count the chopping, extra ingredients, and washing up.The questions we ask before buying A shorter visitThere is a great deal of advice about making the most of a visit. Sometimes that means leaving while everyone is still having a good time.Watching for a while, doing one part, taking a break, or choosing to go home are all things a plan can allow for. Ask about re-entry before you need it.The person taking part should have a say in what comes next. About the links, reviews & languageWe'll tell you what we've tried, what we've only researched, and what didn't work for us.A gift, a hosted stay, paid work, or a commission link will be identified with the post. A gift doesn't buy a good review.Representation matters too. We do not use pity, "inspiration" framing, cure language, or infantilizing content to make disability easier to market. Here is the language standard we hold ourselves to.The planning notes here are family guidance, not individual medical or legal advice. For a correction or question, send us a message. We'd like to get it right.Resource links checked October 2, 2026.

title: The familiar-food plan for days out
summary: The goal is not a perfect restaurant experience. It is knowing what food is available, what you can bring and what the backup is before hunger turns into the hardest part of the day.
search: Outings · FoodThe familiar-food plan for days outThe goal is not a perfect restaurant experience. It is knowing what food is available, what you can bring and what the backup is before hunger turns into the hardest part of the day. In this guideWhat can come inTwo plansWhen to eatNo food battles Check the rules before you pack. Ask whether outside food and drinks are allowed, and whether exceptions are available for disability-related needs when relevant. Keep the answer with the booking or day-out notes. Separate the main meal from the backup. The main meal can be the café, restaurant or food hall you hope to use. The backup is the familiar, practical option that prevents the whole outing from depending on a line, a sold-out item or an unfamiliar menu. Plan the timing, not only the food. Long gaps, unexpected waits and late check-in times can matter more than the menu. Put one reliable eating time into the day plan and keep a portable option for delays. Keep the language neutral. For restrictive eating or strong preferences, focus on access, nutrition guidance from the person’s clinicians when needed, and reducing avoidable stress. A travel guide cannot diagnose feeding difficulties or replace individual care. Keep goingRelated guidesWeekendsPantry kitDay-plan card

title: A little thought before the ribbon.
summary: The best starting point is the person receiving it: what they enjoy, what they use and what will fit comfortably into their life. A gift should feel good to receive.
search: Gifts worth givingA little thought before the ribbon.The best starting point is the person receiving it: what they enjoy, what they use and what will fit comfortably into their life. A gift should feel good to receive.In this guideWrite one sentence about the recipient.Check what comes with the gift.Make the giving easy, too.Need a gift today?Three gifts from a household gift kit · Three photo gifts you can make · The purchased-item notes Write one sentence about the recipient. “They swim every week.” “They love having people over.” “They have asked for a better bag.” A specific, recent detail is a useful place to begin. If the sentence could describe almost anyone, look a little closer or ask a simple question. A wish list is helpful information. So is a request for no gifts. Taste, space and everyday routines matter more than the gift category the calendar suggests. Three good directions Something already wanted. Check the exact version, size or color instead of making the gift into a guessing game.A nicer everyday thing. Consider a well-used category such as a bag, towel or notebook, provided the recipient would welcome a replacement.Something to enjoy and finish. Food, flowers or an outing can suit someone with little space. Confirm their preferences and the practical details first. For teens, begin with their current interests and preferred style. A person who needs help opening, setting up or using a present can still have a clear opinion about what they would like. Check what comes with the gift. The price on the label is only part of the story. A present can quietly arrive with a shopping list, a subscription or a Saturday's worth of assembly. Make the extra work visible before choosing it. Setup: Does it need tools, charging, a separate purchase or an account?Upkeep: Who will wash it, store it, refill it or replace the parts?Ongoing cost: Does useful access require a membership, app payment or regular supplies?Fit: Is there space for it, and can the recipient use its controls and packaging?Flexibility: Can it be exchanged, returned or used at another time? An experience deserves the same care. Check dates, booking requirements, travel, parking, access, expiry and cancellation terms. A ticket may be a lovely gift, but a fixed date should fit the recipient's actual plans. Ask before booking something that commits their time. For a host, choose something that can be enjoyed later. A gift that requires immediate serving, rearranging or finding a vase adds another task just as the doorbell rings. Make the giving easy, too. Set an all-in budget before browsing. Include shipping, wrapping and any essential extra that makes the present usable. A modest gift chosen accurately can be far more welcome than something expensive that misses the person. Teachers, teams and shared thank-yous Check the school or organization's gift policy before collecting money or buying. Keep any group contribution optional and private. A short, specific thank-you can stand on its own; nobody needs to match someone else's spending. Before adding initials Confirm spelling, preferred name, design and delivery timing. Read the return terms for personalized items. If the choice is uncertain, leave room for the recipient to exchange it. Include a gift receipt where possible and make it clear that swapping is welcome. If opening packaging is difficult, ask whether some preparation would help, while keeping the return options in mind. Leave account creation and personal settings to the recipient unless they ask for help. Then let the gift belong to them. They can open it later, enjoy it privately, use it differently than imagined or decide it is not quite right. Thoughtfulness includes that bit of breathing room.

title: The grandparent field notes
summary: Practical field notes for grandparents: comfortable visits, current interests, simple traditions, support you can offer and boundaries that keep plans workable.
search: Family & caregiver field notes / Grandparents Family life · GrandparentsThe grandparent field notesCome make a little tradition that has room to grow with your grandchild.4 minute read · Practical field notesPrint this guide In this guideMeet the person they are now.Ask four useful questions before a visit.Three traditions with an easy smaller version.Make your home easier to visit.Offer the help you can repeat.Stay in touch from farther away.Meet the person they are now. A favorite mug, a particular chair, a short visit at the kitchen table: familiar details can make a welcome feel personal. Ask what your grandchild enjoys now. Their interests, clothes, food preferences and communication may have changed since the last long visit. These ideas are for grandparents and people with a grandparent-like place in someone’s life. Some visit occasionally; some provide everyday care or raise their grandchildren. Choose the parts that fit. You can also use the maternal, paternal and respite notes when those responsibilities are yours. Ask four useful questions before a visit. What would they enjoy? Ask the person directly, with familiar communication support when needed. A recent photograph of an activity or an actual object may help make an option clear.What has changed? Check the practical details you need for this visit rather than relying on last year’s routine.What support is needed? Agree who provides it, what you can safely manage and what somebody else must do.How will we finish? A clear departure time or a short goodbye routine can help everyone plan the rest of the day. Learn where the communication system and backup are kept. Ask for a demonstration if something is unfamiliar. There is no need to know everything on the first visit, but the people providing support need to know the essentials before they take responsibility. Three traditions with an easy smaller version. The same small snack Offer a food and drink that fit the person’s current eating arrangements. Set out the familiar plate or cup if they like it. Let them choose the seat, the music or whether to join you. The smaller version is a short visit without food; hospitality can be a comfortable place to sit. A little look through the photo box Choose a few photographs you have permission to share. Tell one short story and leave room for a response, a question or a change of subject. An older teen or adult may prefer recent photographs, music or a shared interest. Put the box away when the interest ends. Nobody needs to identify every face. The familiar garden round Look at one planter, a bird at the window or a small part of the garden. Make the route fit both people’s mobility and the weather. Bring the needed supports and leave the rest of the garden for another time. An indoor view or a photograph of what has grown works for a short-distance version. Make your home easier to visit. Check the actual route from the car to the place you plan to sit. Ask about steps, bathroom access, seating and any space needed for equipment. Put away items that conflict with the person’s established safety arrangements before they arrive. Keep greetings warm and flexible. Offer a wave or words instead of requiring a hug. Tell other visitors the useful plan, such as the quieter room or early finish, without passing around private care details. A grandchild’s age and preferences should guide gifts and conversation. Offer the help you can repeat. Be specific about your own limits. “I can come for lunch and keep you company, but I cannot manage lifting or the stairs” is useful information. Ask for another suitable person or a different setting when the planned support is beyond what you can do. If you are taking responsibility for care, use the handover guide. A visit as a grandparent does not automatically include sole supervision, transport or personal care. Those tasks need an explicit agreement and the appropriate preparation. Stay in touch from farther away. Try a short call at a useful time, a postcard about an ordinary interest, or one photograph sent through the family’s agreed private channel. Ask which format the person enjoys. A call can be five minutes; a reply can arrive later or in a different form. Before the next visit, write down one thing to repeat and one thing to change. Keep the note kind and practical: “The kitchen was noisy; next time we will sit in the smaller room.” The best tradition is one people still want to return to.Explore all family & caregiver field notes

title: A better hair appointment begins before the chair
summary: The booking questions, haircut brief and small comforts that make a salon appointment easier to use.
search: Home/The library/The little refreshThe little refresh · Guide · 3 minute readA better hair appointment begins before the chairThe booking questions, haircut brief and small comforts that make a salon appointment easier to use.By An AUsome Life · Editorial guidePrint this guideIn this guideWrite a haircut brief that fits on a phone screenBook the service you actually wantSay the comfort part plainlyLeave space around the appointmentA haircut can be a pleasant hour with a magazine and someone else handling the details. It can also involve a noisy dryer, an unfamiliar sink, a long wait and a conversation that leaves everybody agreeing to something slightly different. The useful preparation is specific: decide what you want done, what you want to skip and what would make the visit comfortable. This is an appointment-planning guide. It does not name a family-tested salon or prescribe a haircut for anyone else's hair. A good fit includes the person in the chair, the stylist's skills and the actual service being booked. Write a haircut brief that fits on a phone screen Bring one or two reference pictures and explain the feature you mean. It might be the length at the neck, the way the fringe sits or the amount of hair left around the ears. A reference picture contains plenty of other information, including texture and styling, that may have little to do with your own hair. Ask the stylist what is achievable and what the daily upkeep would involve. Add the ordinary-day constraint. Perhaps you want to wash and go, tie it back, wear a hat comfortably or spend only a few minutes styling. Those details give the conversation somewhere practical to begin. Save room for professional advice without treating a photograph as a promise. Book the service you actually want Ask what the appointment includes: consultation, wash, cut, drying and styling. Confirm the expected length of the appointment and the total for the agreed service. If you would rather leave without a blow-dry, ask whether that is available and how it affects the booking. Do the same for optional treatments before they begin. For Massachusetts readers, the state's salon consumer guidance explains the licensing framework. The official license lookup is a useful basic check. A license is not a personal recommendation, and a beautiful social feed does not answer appointment-specific questions. Say the comfort part plainly A short request is often clearer than a long explanation. “Could you tell me before turning on the dryer?” “Can we agree on the length before you begin?” “I prefer a quiet appointment.” “Please give me a moment to answer.” The salon can then say what it can accommodate. If the visit is for someone who uses communication support, address them directly and keep that support available. Ask about permission before sharing personal information with staff. A list of useful preferences usually serves the appointment better than a public account of someone's difficulties. A support person can help explain the plan while leaving room for the client's own choices. Leave space around the appointment Choose a time that does not force a race between commitments. Ask whether the first appointment of the day is usually quieter, rather than assuming it is. Check parking and the route into the building if either affects the visit. A quiet waiting area, an alternative to waiting inside or a chance to pause may matter more than the refreshments menu. Before leaving, take a moment to look at the result in the way you will normally wear it. Ask how to manage the chosen style with the tools already at home. Write down only the details worth repeating: stylist, service, useful wording and preferred booking time. A little continuity can make the next appointment much simpler, without turning personal care into a project.Sources & editorial notesReviewed October 2026. title: A photo box with a story you can find again
summary: A manageable first pass through printed photographs, with careful handling, useful context and a small finished collection.
search: Home/The library/At homeAt home · Guide · 3 minute readA photo box with a story you can find againA manageable first pass through printed photographs, with careful handling, useful context and a small finished collection.By An AUsome Life · Editorial guidePrint this guideIn this guideSet up a small, clear work areaGive the group a simple identityAsk one specific questionPreserve the ordinary contextChoose a sensible place to keep itFinish one small collectionA box of photographs is often several projects at once. There are pictures to identify, duplicates to sort, relatives to ask and albums you may eventually want to make. Start smaller: choose one event, one year or one modest stack, and make that part easier to understand and find. The first goal is a usable little collection. You can decide about the grand family archive another day. Set up a small, clear work area Keep food and drinks away from the photographs. The Library of Congress recommends careful handling, avoiding the image surface, and labeling suitable housing materials instead of marking photographs where possible. Its guidance also warns against adhesives and mechanical fasteners on prints and recommends photo-safe enclosures. For fragile, damaged or unfamiliar photographic materials, read the full guidance or ask a qualified conservator before attempting treatment. Work with a small group that can be safely put away at the end of the session. A project left spread across the dining table can become much larger than intended when the room needs to be used again. Give the group a simple identity Choose a name that another person could understand: “Seaside weekend, summer 2019” is more useful than “old favorites.” If the date or place is uncertain, say so. A question mark preserves an honest gap; a confident guess can become mistaken family history. Create a separate note with the people, place, approximate date and source of the information. Keep each photograph associated with the right note through an appropriate enclosure or simple inventory. Avoid numbering or sticking labels directly onto the print unless you have confirmed a suitable method for that material. Ask one specific question If a relative might recognize a picture, make the question easy. “Do you remember which beach this was?” gives them a starting point. “Tell me everything about the family photos” is a much bigger request. Let them distinguish memory from inference, and record whose recollection it is. Permission matters when sharing copies, especially photographs involving children or private moments. A request for help identifying one picture does not require sending the entire album. Keep the circle as small as the task needs. Preserve the ordinary context An archive benefits from details beyond formal occasions. A shop sign, the layout of a room or the name of a favorite book can help explain a period of life. Write down the things you genuinely know, and separate them from feelings or reactions you would be inventing for someone else. A caption can be very short: where, when, who and why this particular picture was kept. If the photograph will eventually appear publicly, create a separate public caption. Leave private identities, precise routines and sensitive details in the private record when there is a legitimate reason to keep them at all. Choose a sensible place to keep it The Library of Congress emphasizes a cool, relatively dry, stable storage environment, away from light, leaks and extremes. It advises against attics and basements and identifies standards for photo-safe sleeves and boxes. Follow the guidance appropriate to your materials rather than assuming every product labeled “archival” is equivalent. A decorative box can still be useful for an outer layer, but check what touches the photograph. Keep the collection somewhere it can be retrieved without unpacking half a cupboard. Finish one small collection Make a brief inventory of what you have completed and what remains uncertain. If you make digital copies, give them matching names and check that they actually open. Keep original files intact when experimenting with edits. The finished result might be only twenty photographs and a page of notes. That is enough to turn an anonymous pile into something another family member can understand. It also gives the next session a clear beginning, which is often the best reason to stop while the work still feels pleasant.Sources & editorial notesReviewed October 2026.
